summary: In EVPN, the Designated Forwarder is the router responsible for sending broadcast, unknown unicast, and multicast traffic to a multihomed network. This RFC defines a preference-based way to elect the Designated Forwarder, letting operators influence which router is chosen.

plainLanguage.summary: Several helpers could carry the mail but only one should. This gives each helper a priority number so the choice is predictable.

questions: how is the evpn df chosen
what is the evpn designated forwarder
what is highest preference df election
what does don't preempt mean in evpn
what is the default df preference value
subtitle: A way for EVPN operators to choose, by preference number, which router forwards flooded traffic for a multihomed site.

tldr.problem: The default Designated Forwarder election in EVPN is automatic, so operators cannot easily say which router should win, force a switchover for maintenance, or stop a recovered router from taking over again.
tldr.mechanism: Two new DF algorithms, Highest-Preference and Lowest-Preference, rank the routers on an Ethernet Segment by a 2-octet preference carried in the DF Election Extended Community. A "Don't Preempt" bit adds non-revertive behavior.
tldr.outcome: Operators get deterministic, configurable control over DF election and can avoid needless traffic loss when a failed router returns. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 8584.

today: RFC 9785 is a Proposed Standard from June 2025 and updates RFC 8584 by changing the definition of the DF Election Extended Community. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Problem: Who Forwards Flooded Traffic
sections.content:
In an Ethernet Virtual Private Network (EVPN), a customer device or network can be attached to several Provider Edge (PE) routers at once. Among the PEs that advertise the same Ethernet Segment Identifier (ESI), one is chosen as the Designated Forwarder (DF). It sends Broadcast, Unknown Unicast and Multicast (BUM) traffic to the multihomed site, and also unicast traffic in the Single-Active case.

The default algorithm and the Highest Random Weight (HRW) algorithm from RFC 8584 pick the DF automatically across Ethernet Tags. That is efficient, but some operators need a more user-controlled method. They also want an easy way to force a switchover for maintenance, and a way to control whether a new active PE can preempt the existing DF.
sections.plainLanguage: When several routers could do the same job, a rule picks one. The old rule picked automatically, and people wanted a way to say who should go first.

sections.title: What the Solution Must Do
sections.content:
The RFC lists five requirements the procedures meet:

  • An administrative preference, so the operator decides whether the highest or lowest preference among the PEs becomes DF.
  • Support for Ethernet Segments from RFC 7432 and virtual Ethernet Segments from RFC 9784.
  • Forcing a PE to preempt the DF for an Ethernet Tag just by changing its preference, without reconfiguring every PE.
  • An optional Don't Preempt capability, giving non-revertive behavior even if the former DF comes back after a failure. The election in RFC 7432 is always revertive.
  • Support for Single-Active and All-Active multihoming.
sections.plainLanguage: The wish list: let people choose the order, let them change the boss without redoing everything, and let the new boss stay boss when the old one comes back.

sections.title: The DF Election Extended Community
sections.content:
The solution reuses the DF Election Extended Community from RFC 8584, which travels with the Ethernet Segment route. When the DF algorithm is Highest-Preference or Lowest-Preference, the last two reserved octets become a DF Preference field. This is why the RFC updates RFC 8584.

The DF Alg field gets two new values: 2 for the Highest-Preference Algorithm and 3 for the Lowest-Preference Algorithm. Alg 0 is the default modulus-based algorithm and Alg 1 is HRW.

The preference is a 2-octet value from 0 to 65535, and the default MUST be 32767, the midpoint, so operators have room above and below. The 2-octet Bitmap carries capabilities. Bit 0 is the D (Don't Preempt) bit, with a default of 0 meaning normal revertive behavior. Bit 1 is the AC-Influenced DF bit from RFC 8584, which MAY be combined with these algorithms. The RSV and Reserved bits are set to zero on sending and ignored on receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router attaches a little note to its announcement. The note says which rule it uses, how important it is (a number), and whether it wants to keep its job once it has it.

sections.title: Highest- and Lowest-Preference Election
sections.content:
Each PE advertises an Ethernet Segment route carrying three parameters, written (Pref, DP, Alg). After the DF Wait timer expires, each PE checks that all Ethernet Segment routes, including its own, use the same algorithm. If they are a mix, even Highest versus Lowest, the procedure falls back to the default DF algorithm of RFC 7432.

With Highest-Preference, the PEs are ordered from the numerically highest preference to the lowest and the first one is the DF. With Lowest-Preference the order is reversed. In the RFC's example, vES1 has preferences 500 on PE1 and 255 on PE2, so PE1 is DF under Highest-Preference and PE2 under Lowest-Preference.

If preferences are equal, an implementation MUST first prefer the PE advertising Don't Preempt, then the PE with the lowest IP address, taken from the Originating Router's IP address. An IPv4 address counts as lower than an IPv6 address.

For maintenance, the operator can change a PE's preference, for example PE3 from 300 to 50, and another PE takes over regardless of Don't Preempt. The preference MUST be configured per Ethernet Segment, and local policy MAY change it dynamically, for example when a port in a link aggregation group is lost. The policies themselves are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone shouts a number. With the highest-number rule the biggest number wins, with the lowest-number rule the smallest wins. If there is a tie, the one who asked to be left alone wins, then the one with the smaller address.

sections.title: Spreading Load Across Ethernet Tags
sections.content:
On a plain Ethernet Segment that can hold thousands of Ethernet Tags, using one of these algorithms for everything makes the same PE the DF for all tags. To balance load, the signaled algorithm MAY be overridden by a local policy for a range of Ethernet Tags.

In the RFC's example, PE1 is (500, 0, Highest-Preference) and PE2 is (100, 0, Highest-Preference) for ES3, and both are configured with Lowest-Preference for tags 2001-4000. PE1 becomes DF for tags 1-2000 and PE2 for tags 2001-4000. With three or more PEs this gives only two DFs, so virtual Ethernet Segments are RECOMMENDED when good balancing is wanted.

Any such override MUST be consistent on every PE of the segment. If it is not, packets may be dropped or duplicated on the affected Ethernet Tag.
sections.plainLanguage: If one helper would carry all the mail, you can tell some helpers to use the opposite rule for some streets, so two helpers share the work. Everyone must agree on which streets, or mail gets lost or sent twice.

sections.title: The Non-Revertive Capability
sections.content:
Normally, if the DF fails and later returns, it takes over again, which can cause unnecessary packet loss. The Don't Preempt capability prevents that. It is set per PE and per Ethernet Segment, and PEs on a segment should be configured consistently, though the RFC does not enforce it. If they are inconsistent, non-revertive behavior is not guaranteed.

When a PE's Ethernet Segment recovers, it waits on a boot-timer or hold-timer, applied between the INIT and DF_WAIT states of the state machine in RFC 8584. It then selects a reference PE: the "Highest-PE" and, if a local policy overrides the algorithm for some tags, also a "Lowest-PE". Ties are broken by Don't Preempt (DP=1 is better) and then the lower PE IP address.

The returning PE compares its own preference with those PEs. If it would win, it advertises an operational "in-use" preference equal to the reference PE's, with DP=0. This causes no DF change, because Don't Preempt acts as a tiebreaker. In the example, PE3 with administrative preference 300 advertises (200, 0) after seeing PE2. If PE2 later fails and PE3 becomes the new Highest-PE, PE3 sends its administrative (300, 1) and becomes DF.

If a returning PE advertises a different DF algorithm from the other PEs, all PEs MUST fall back to the default algorithm, whatever Don't Preempt says.
sections.plainLanguage: When the old boss returns, it quietly says it has the same number as the current boss instead of a bigger one. So the current boss keeps the job until it is really needed to change.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The preference algorithms give absolute control, by configuration, over which PE is DF for a given Ethernet Tag. An attacker who can change the configuration of a PE could therefore change the preference and affect the traffic through that PE and segment, which is not possible with an automated algorithm such as HRW.

Non-revertive behavior may be seen as a security improvement, since intentional link or node flapping only disrupts service once. But an attacker with configuration access can disable it by advertising a conflicting DF algorithm and forcing the fallback. Inconsistent local policies can cause packet drops or duplication. The algorithms do not change how PEs share Ethernet Segment information, so the security considerations of RFC 7432 and RFC 8584 still apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Because a person sets the numbers, a bad person with access could change them to steer the mail. The old automatic rule was harder to steer.

sections.title: IANA Allocations
sections.content: IANA allocated values 2 (Highest-Preference Algorithm) and 3 (Lowest-Preference Algorithm) in the "DF Alg" registry created by RFC 8584. It also allocated bit 0, the D (Don't Preempt) Capability, in the "DF Election Capabilities" registry. It listed RFC 9785 as an additional reference for Sub-Type 0x06, the DF Election Extended Community.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of rule numbers got two new entries and one new checkbox.
